title: Chat generation basics: setup, retries, streaming + Console tour
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted chat/text generation. Covered streaming behavior, retry/backoff patterns, key generation params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), console tooling for requests and traces, and initial POC next steps. Customer concerned about latency, payload residency, and audit logs. Agreed to run a 1-week pilot with sample workload and follow-up benchmark session.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~38m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Marcus (BlueOak CTO), Aisha (Lead ML Eng), Tom (Product), Lina (Infra)
Links referenced: [deck] https://redwood.ai/decks/hosted-chat-intro, [security packet] https://redwood.ai/security/packet, [benchmark template] shared in chat

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is Sofia our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
00:12 Marcus: Doing well, thanks. Got a few folks from infra and product today to talk through latency and compliance.
00:18 Jordan: Great. The plan is quick 10 minute intro, live demo of hosted chat generation and streaming, then dive into retries and console traces, and end with next steps. Sound ok?
00:29 Marcus: Yep.
00:33 Sofia: All right jumping in, i'll share my screen — sorry the deck's up — first slide just what hosted API gives you, simple REST/SDK, streaming, and we also have the console for live tracing.
00:48 Sofia: Quick note, transcription may show some names wrong, god sorry, small typo — but anyway.
01:02 Sofia: When you call /v1/chat, you get chunked streaming by default for streaming endpoints, you can set partial tokens to appear as they generate. If the connection drops we have recommended retry behaviors that don't double-send completions — we'll demo.
01:22 Tom: Can you explain what you mean by "partial tokens"? Is that subtoken or chunk?
01:29 Sofia: Sure, partial tokens mean the server will flush incremental tokens as they are emitted. Sometimes clients see mid-word fragments if chunking boundaries fall in the middle of a UTF-8 sequence, which is why we recommend a little client buffering to avoid showing halves if that's undesirable.
01:47 Aisha: That matches what we saw with another provider — we get mid-word partials and want to ensure user UX doesn't show garbage. Do you have a flag to control flush frequency?
01:57 Sofia: Yes there's a streaming_sample_rate and flush_threshold for SDKs, default to UX-friendly values, and you can tune to reduce latency at cost of a few partials.
02:12 Jordan: Quick architecture point: hosted API is routed through our runtime, which selects kernels and handles KV cache and batching. For most chat apps you get prefix caching improvements if many users hit similar system prompts.
02:29 Lina: For our compliance team, can you confirm data residency and retention on hosted? We need logs for 90 days and an option for redaction.
02:38 Jordan: Good question. By default transient request logs expire after 30 days but we have enterprise retention options and a private deployment for strict residency. We'll put the SOC2 and retention options in the security packet — action item for me.
02:52 Marcus: Cool.
02:58 Sofia: I'll switch to a live API demo — curl first then the console. Curl: 
03:05 Sofia: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat -H "Authorization: Bearer <KEY>" -d '{"messages":[{"role":"system","content":"You are concise"},{"role":"user","content":"Summarize Q2 revenue highlights"}],"max_tokens":150,"temperature":0.2}'
03:33 Sofia: That returns a streaming response, you see token events as they arrive. If the client gets a connection error we recommend an idempotent restart: replay up to the last confirmed token or use message-level idempotency keys to avoid duplicates.
03:53 Tom: How do you recommend handling retries if the client reconnects and we already rendered partial text to the user?
03:59 Sofia: Common pattern: checkpoint the last confirmed token index, on reconnect request only tokens after that index. We also support message_id idempotency so server can ignore duplicate messages.
04:13 Aisha: Is idempotency built into the hosted API or the SDK?
04:18 Sofia: Both. The API supports idempotency keys as a header. SDKs expose helpers that store local checkpoint state.
04:27 Jordan: Now i'll hop to the console to show traces, cost breakdowns, and request/response timeline.
04:36 Sofia: On screen you can see the request timing, token counts, and per-token latency spikes. The console shows the model variant used and if a fallback was triggered.
04:50 Sofia: [console view] Here's a request that fell back from quantized variant to full fp16 when latency threshold was tight; we log reason codes.
05:06 Marcus: That fallback — can we pin a model version so we don't get unexpected quality changes?
05:12 Jordan: Absolutely — customers can pin model versions and disable automatic fallbacks if they prefer. We recommend canarying changes first.
05:22 Aisha: What about batching — will that add unpredictable latency spikes?
05:28 Sofia: We have continuous batching which batches very small windows by default to minimize tail latency. You can tune batching windows or disable batching if you need strictly single-request latency, but at cost increase.
05:41 Tom: Do you expose batching debug traces?
05:44 Sofia: Yes the console shows batch composition and why requests waited — e.g., waiting for KV cache, model warmup, or to fill a batch.
05:55 Jordan: Let's demo an induced network error and show retries. I'll trigger a disconnect on the client side.
06:05 [sound of keyboard clacks]
06:08 Sofia: Ok simulating a network reset — you can see the client got a ECONNRESET at 06:08; client attempts reconnect with linear backoff 500ms, 1s, 2s.
06:20 Sofia: The console shows the reconnect events and whether the server accepted a replay based on idempotency key.
06:29 Marcus: If the reconnection fails repeatedly, do you have a fallback model in another region to reduce cross-region latency?
06:36 Jordan: Yes routing policies can fallback to a nearby region or a lower-cost variant. You can specify priority policies per route.
06:47 Aisha: For our POC we plan to simulate 500 concurrent users with avg 120 tokens/session, 10 rps sustained. Any immediate red flags?
06:57 Sofia: That workload is well within hosted API but you'll want a dedicated pool for predictable SLAs if concurrency grows. For a one-week pilot hosted should be fine, we can provision dedicated if you see degradation.
07:12 Marcus: What's the unit cost model? Token based?
07:16 Jordan: Hosted pricing is per input and per output token with tiers. We'll include a sample cost calc for your traffic profile.
07:26 Tom: Can we see a trace where a streaming packet got duplicated by a bad client retry?
07:31 Sofia: Yep here's a trace where client retried without idempotency key — you can see duplicate token events and our console flags it as potential duplicate.
07:43 Sofia: The recommended fix is to use an idempotency header or checkpoint the confirmed token index.
07:51 Lina: On the security front, how do you do encryption at rest and KMS integration?
07:57 Jordan: We integrate with customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. For hosted we use AES-256 at rest and rotate keys; enterprise customers can opt for bring-your-own-key in Dedicated/Private.
08:12 Aisha: Do you provide audit logs for all requests?
08:16 Jordan: Yes, audit logs are available and can be streamed to S3 or a SIEM, and retained to your required retention policy under enterprise plans.
08:27 Marcus: Any SOC2 or ISO certs to share now?
08:30 Jordan: Yes SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 — i'll share the packet after this call.
08:36 Sofia: Back to params — temperature, top_p, and max_tokens. For deterministic responses set temp to 0 or use top_p tuning. We'll demo how temperature changes output variance.
08:51 Sofia: [demo prompt] "Write a concise bullet list of regulatory risks for a payments startup" with temp 0.2 vs temp 0.9.
09:03 Sofia: Temp 0.2 yields tighter, safer list; 0.9 yields more variety and occasionally hallucinated items. For financial customer we generally recommend lower temp and guardrails.
09:18 Aisha: Guardrails — do you offer pre-output filters or content safety hooks?
09:23 Sofia: We have pre- and post-generation filters, plus a reranking endpoint to de-prioritize undesirable outputs. You can also plug in a small safety model as a post-filter.
09:34 Tom: Can the console run evaluations on prompt sets to detect regressions over model upgrades?
09:38 Sofia: Yes Redwood Optimize allows you to register prompt sets, run A/Bs and quality monitoring; it will alert on regressions and surface diffed outputs.
09:50 Marcus: Sounds good. For the pilot we'll need simple runbook: how to collect traces, what prometheus metrics, and example retry settings.
09:59 Jordan: We'll include a runbook in the benchmark template.
10:05 Sofia: One more note on streaming: some clients do not support chunked HTTP well; we provide WebSocket and SSE clients to improve UX.
10:16 Lina: Do you have guidance for mobile clients with flaky networks?
10:20 Sofia: Mobile pattern: show partials but checkpoint confirmed tokens after a short pause (250-500ms). On reconnect use idempotency keys and server-side replay support.
10:33 Marcus: Any limitations on max_tokens per request?
10:36 Sofia: Hosted supports up to 4096 tokens by default, extended windows available on request. For long contexts we recommend KV prefix caching to keep performance stable.
10:48 Aisha: For our compliance we need redaction of sensitive fields in logs — is that automatic?
10:53 Jordan: We can apply auto-redaction heuristics or customers can provide PII patterns. We'll include redaction options in the security packet.
11:06 Sofia: Ok switching to an intentional failure scenario — will show a fallback to a quantized variant to save cost and then a forced full model for quality.
11:20 Sofia: [demo run] Request started at 11:20 — quantized variant returned, then at token 42 a quality threshold triggered a fallback; console marks fallback event and shows reason code FQ-01 (quality threshold low).
11:36 Tom: So the app sees a short pause while fallback loads?
11:40 Sofia: Yes there can be a small increase in latency while the full model warms; we recommend canarying and making fallbacks explicit in UX.
11:50 Marcus: Can you pin to never fallback?
11:52 Jordan: Yes pinning is available per-route. We can also give an SLA-backed dedicated pool if you need zero fallback behavior.
12:02 Aisha: For the pilot we'll probably accept brief fallbacks as long as we can detect them in logs.
12:08 Sofia: Good — console will emit an event you can subscribe to, and Optimize will surface any quality regressions tied to prompt IDs.
12:18 Jordan: Quick Q from chat: customer asked about function calling and structured outputs — do we support function schemas?
12:25 Sofia: Yes our chatgen supports function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs, plus model-assisted extraction. We stream partial JSON as it builds but recommend post-parse validation.
12:40 Tom: If we use function calling heavily, does that change latency characteristics?
12:44 Sofia: Slightly — additional round trips to your tool endpoints add latency, but we often batch some calls and cache calls results where appropriate.
12:55 Marcus: For the POC we'd appreciate simple sample code for Go and Python with streaming reconnection best practices.
13:02 Jordan: We'll include those in the quickstart zip.
13:08 Sofia: We're about 13 minutes in — do you want to go deeper into a performance test or leave for the benchmark call?
13:14 Marcus: Let's leave heavy perf tests for the follow-up; show us the console trace export and where to find cost breakdowns.
13:21 Sofia: On the console export panel you can export traces to JSON or push to S3 and we have a cost dashboard that shows token split by model and route.
13:33 Aisha: Can we subscribe to alerts when cost exceeds a threshold?
13:36 Jordan: Yes, monthly budget alerts and per-route thresholds.
13:42 Sofia: One last demo of a reconnect flow: I will forcibly drop network then reconnect with idempotency header present so server will resume rather than duplicate.
13:52 [simulated disconnect sound]
13:55 Sofia: Reconnect attempt 1 - 500ms, 2 - 1s, 3 - 2s; server accepted replay and timeline shows resumed stream from token 38.
14:11 Marcus: Nice.
14:14 Tom: Any gotchas with webhooks or push callbacks?
14:18 Sofia: If you use webhooks for asynchronous generations, secure endpoints and sign payloads; retries use at-least-once and include delivery ids. We recommend idempotent handlers.
14:33 Aisha: Ok let's talk timeline — we want to start a week-long pilot next week if possible.
14:38 Jordan: We can provision trial keys and a sandbox project by Friday.
14:44 Marcus: Perfect.
14:47 Sofia: I'll note the expected pilot profile: 500 concurrent users, 120 tokens avg, 10 rps — we'll use that for initial cost/capacity planning.
15:02 Jordan: Any other questions?
15:06 Lina: One last infra question: for private deployments, how much ops involvement on our side?
15:13 Jordan: Private has a customer-managed control plane option and an on-prem package; we'll provide deployment scripts and an operator-runbook. For full on-prem you will need node provisioning and networking setup, we do the rest.
15:29 Marcus: And for SSO and RBAC?
15:33 Jordan: We support SAML SSO and granular RBAC; we'll include the SAML metadata example in the security doc.
15:43 Tom: That's all from product.
15:46 Jordan: Great. Recap of next steps: Jordan send quickstart and security packet, Sofia prepare benchmark harness and sample prompts, customer provide traffic profile, schedule follow-up.
15:58 Marcus: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
16:02 Jordan: Thanks, we'll follow up by EOD with links and schedule a benchmark planning call for next week.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality: a few words mis-recognized (e.g., "KV cache" sometimes as "K-V cash"), some punctuation missing, occasional speaker label confusion, overall medium quality.
